title: Blessing after eating (Deuteronomy 8:10)
hookLine: the one blessing the Torah itself commands: eat, be satisfied, and bless

lines: THE LAST PLATE OF A BIG MEAL.
A FULL PERSON TENDS TO FORGET.
cards: The last plate of a big meal. Thanksgiving, a wedding, a birthday dinner. Belts feel tight.
Someone's already clearing the table. Everybody's drifting toward the couch or the car. A hungry person will thank anyone for a piece of bread.
A full one tends to forget. Here's a surprise about Jewish blessings over food: the blessings before eating were set by the rabbis. The one blessing the Torah itself commands comes after.
Today: Birkat Hamazon, the blessing after eating.

teach.b: The verse is in Deuteronomy, in the old Jewish Publication Society translation: "And thou shalt eat and be satisfied, and bless the LORD thy God for the good land which He hath given thee." Eat. Be satisfied.

A few verses later, the Torah warns: when you've eaten and are satisfied, and built good houses, and your flocks and silver and gold have grown, be careful that your heart doesn't grow proud and forget.
The Torah's worry is plain: hunger remembers, fullness forgets. So the blessing sits right at the moment you're most likely to skip it. Birkat hamazon means the blessing for food.
It's a longer grace, with four main blessings, and the Talmud gives each one a history. The first, for God who feeds the whole world, it credits to Moses, when the manna fell.
The second, for the land, to Joshua, when the people entered it. The third, for Jerusalem, to David and Solomon.
The fourth, for God who is good and does good, the rabbis added after a terrible defeat, when the bodies of the fallen were finally allowed burial: a thanks said even out of grief.
So one after-dinner grace carries the whole story from the desert to the rabbis.

teach.h: THREE AT A TABLE: LET US BLESS.
teach.b: When three or more eat together, one person invites the others to bless, and they answer, like a small congregation around a table.
On Shabbat and holidays the custom is to begin by singing a psalm about coming home from exile. After smaller snacks there are shorter blessings.
But the idea is the same: when you're full, that's the moment to say thank you.

how: After a meal with bread, observant Jews say Birkat Hamazon, often led by one person when three or more have eaten together; after other foods they say a shorter blessing.

o: a toast offered to the host at a festive dinner
the grace said after eating, once you're full
a compliment paid to the cook

games.q: what's inside the grace — tap the pairs.

s: the Torah commands a blessing before eating
the Torah commands the blessing after: eat, be satisfied, and bless. the ones before were set by the rabbis.
the Torah warns that fullness makes people forget
when you've eaten and are satisfied, be careful your heart doesn't grow proud.
the fourth blessing was added after a time of grief
the rabbis added it when the fallen of a terrible defeat were finally allowed burial.

games.q: you're reading Deuteronomy. the Torah wants people to thank God for food. when does it say to bless?
o: before the first bite, when you're hungry.
after you've eaten and are satisfied.
games.why: "thou shalt eat and be satisfied, and bless": after, because fullness is when people forget.

practice: Think back to the last thing you ate: where did it come from, who grew it, carried it, cooked it, and how did it feel to be full, or at least not hungry?
If you pray, you can offer thanks to God for it now, in your own words, or with the old verse: eat, be satisfied, and bless. If you don't, simply thank whoever made the meal possible, in your mind.

wordCard.voice: Birkat Hamazon. The blessing after eating: the one food blessing the Torah itself commands, said when you're full.

orig.note: Hebrew: the blessing for food. mazon means food, nourishment.

carryVoice: Your line: full, then grateful. The Torah's own food blessing waits until after the meal. See you tomorrow.
